title: 2 Chronicles 18:28–34
context: 2 Chronicles 18:28–34 parallels 1 Kings 22:29–35. Ahab disguises himself while Jehoshaphat wears his robes, the Syrian chariot captains are ordered to fight only with the king of Israel, and they pursue Jehoshaphat until they see he is not Ahab. Chronicles adds that when Jehoshaphat cried out, “the LORD helped him; and God moved them to depart from him” (18:31), where Kings says only that “Jehoshaphat cried out” before the captains turn back. Chronicles does not give the number of captains found in Kings, and it ends with Ahab’s death without the scattering of the army, the burial, or the dogs licking his blood (1 Kings 22:36–38). Both traditions read the section as shared ground: the LORD’s word through Micaiah is fulfilled, and the LORD mercifully preserves Jehoshaphat.

verses.text: So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah went up to Ramoth Gilead.
verses.arminianNotes:
So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah go up to Ramoth Gilead. The wording matches Kings.

Arminian readers note that both kings go ahead despite Micaiah’s clear warning, and that Jehoshaphat, who asked for the LORD’s word, does not act on it, a sobering example of a believer’s real and costly choice.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see both kings walking into the judgment that was announced, and they note that Jehoshaphat’s participation will be rebuked by Jehu son of Hanani in 19:2.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 22:29: hearing God’s word and still going one’s own way is a danger for the faithful as well as for the faithless.

verses.text: The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “I will disguise myself, and go into the battle; but you put on your robes.” So the king of Israel disguised himself; and they went into the battle.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Israel says he will disguise himself and go into battle, while Jehoshaphat puts on his robes, and the king of Israel disguises himself. He tries to evade the word.

Arminian readers note that Ahab tries to escape the prophecy while leaving his ally exposed, and that the disguise shows he took the warning more seriously than he admitted.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a futile attempt to escape what the LORD has spoken, and they note that the plan places Jehoshaphat in the danger meant for Ahab, setting up the LORD’s rescue in 18:31.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: human schemes cannot overturn what the LORD has spoken, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 22:30.

verses.text: Now the king of Syria had commanded the captains of his chariots, saying, “Don’t fight with small nor great, except only with the king of Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Syria has commanded the captains of his chariots to fight with no one, small or great, except the king of Israel. Chronicles does not give the number of captains that Kings gives.

Arminian readers note that the order targets Ahab, though the text gives no motive, and that it leaves Jehoshaphat, still in his robes, exposed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the scene arranged so that Ahab’s fate will be clear, and they note that the command sets up the danger to Jehoshaphat and his deliverance in the next verse.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 22:31, and they record the absence of “thirty-two captains” in Chronicles without harmonizing it.

verses.text: When the captains of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat, they said, “It is the king of Israel!” Therefore they turned around to fight against him. But Jehoshaphat cried out, and the LORD helped him; and God moved them to depart from him.
verses.arminianNotes:
The captains see Jehoshaphat, say, “It is the king of Israel!” and turn to fight him, “But Jehoshaphat cried out, and the LORD helped him; and God moved them to depart from him.” Kings has only “they came over to fight against him. Jehoshaphat cried out.”

Arminian readers see God answering a cry for help with real mercy, even after an unwise choice.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s governing hand even over the movements of enemy captains, protecting his servant despite the danger he walked into.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 22:32: God can rescue his people from the consequences of an unwise decision, though they should not presume on it. Neither builds a contrast on the verse.

verses.text: When the captains of the chariots saw that it was not the king of Israel, they turned back from pursuing him.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the captains see that it is not the king of Israel, they turn back from pursuing him. The rescue is complete.

Arminian readers note Jehoshaphat’s deliverance as an act of mercy, and they observe that the disguise meant to protect Ahab nearly cost Jehoshaphat his life, a sober reminder of the cost of his alliance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the LORD’s preserving care for the king of Judah, and in Chronicles they read the captains’ turning back as the outworking of God moving them away in the previous verse.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 22:33: God is merciful to his servant in a moment of danger.

verses.text: A certain man drew his bow at random, and struck the king of Israel between the joints of the armor. Therefore he said to the driver of the chariot, “Turn around and carry me out of the battle, for I am severely wounded.”
verses.arminianNotes:
A certain man draws his bow at random and strikes the king of Israel between the joints of the armor, and the king tells the driver of the chariot to carry him out of the battle. Kings has “the driver of his chariot”.

Arminian readers note that the archer acts freely and without aim, yet the word of the LORD is fulfilled through an ordinary human action.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see providence guiding even an arrow shot at random (compare Proverbs 16:33), so that the disguise could not hide Ahab from the LORD’s word.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 22:34, though they describe how God governs such events in different terms, as discussed at Judges 9:23.

verses.text: The battle increased that day. However, the king of Israel propped himself up in his chariot against the Syrians until the evening; and at about sunset, he died.
verses.arminianNotes:
The battle increases, and the king of Israel props himself up in his chariot against the Syrians until evening, and at about sunset he dies. Kings says he “was propped up” and adds that the blood ran into the chariot.

Arminian readers note the sober detail of his death, facing the enemy as the prophecy foretold.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the fulfillment of Micaiah’s word that the king would not return in peace (18:27), and they note that Chronicles ends the account here, without the burial or the dogs licking his blood (1 Kings 22:37–38).

Both traditions read the death soberly as God’s judgment, not with triumph, and they record the differences from Kings without harmonizing them.
